The Long Way Home

Meet the bogong moth: a dusty brown night flier that grows up on inland plains, then migrates hundreds of kilometres to cool alpine caves, and later returns north to breed again. This page turns the story into a hands-on mini exhibit.

Touch: drag the moth, tap the stars, and explore each stage.
Listen: enable narration and a gentle synthesized soundscape.
Learn: short facts are written for kids and curious grown-ups.
Drag me through the night sky
Bogong moths are famous for long migrations at night. Tap the sky to make star sparks, then drag the moth around to see it glide.

Life begins here

Tap a card to open the next chapter of the moth’s life. Then tap the big specimen image to make it wiggle and replay the bite-sized explanation.

Stage

Eggs

Fly to the mountains

Drag the moth from the inland breeding grounds to the Australian Alps. The progress meter fills as you approach the mountains. When the moth reaches the cave, you’ll unlock the summer resting stage.

Plains
Alps
Start on the plains. Young bogong moths develop inland, then many adults migrate south-east to cool mountain caves for summer aestivation — a kind of dormancy.

How does it find the way?

Scientists have shown that bogong moths can use the night sky and Earth’s magnetic field together. Turn cues on and off to see how the flying dots behave.

Stars
With visible stars, the moths in our toy simulation fly in a more consistent direction.
Magnetic cue
Earth’s magnetic field gives another orientation clue. The real moths seem to combine this with celestial information.
City lights
Artificial light can attract and disrupt night-flying insects. Here, it pulls some moths off course.
Both cues are on, so the swarm is travelling in a steady, purposeful direction.

Remember these things

Short, memorable facts to take away.

Night traveller

Bogong moths are strongly associated with nocturnal migration. Their brown camouflage helps them hide by day.

Summer sleeper

In mountain caves, many adults cluster together and aestivate during the hot months — resting until conditions change.

Important food web link

The moths have long been ecologically and culturally significant in alpine Australia, including as food for animals and people.

Science notes: Based on the 2025 Nature study on stellar and magnetic navigation and Australian moth ecology. The moth and life-stage artwork is AI-generated educational illustration, not diagnostic scientific photography.

This interactive page is educational and illustrative. It reflects well-established broad biology of Agrotis infusa and the now widely discussed evidence that bogong moths can use stellar and magnetic information for navigation. Some details can vary by population and year, so the page simplifies a complex natural story for an easy, engaging overview.
